# Fieldwork safety

These are the rules the group holds itself to when working on site, not general
advice handed down from somewhere else. Nobody is exempt from them because they're in
a hurry or the weather looks fine from the car park.

## Working alone

Nobody climbs a mast alone, full stop, regardless of how quick the job is meant to
be. If a second person isn't available for a mast job, the job waits for a weekend
when one is. This applies even to a five-minute check that "doesn't really count" as
climbing.

## Weather cut-offs

No mast work in wind over 30 mph, gauged by feel and the state of the trees rather
than a forecast checked that morning, since the forecast and the actual wind on an
exposed ridge often disagree. No mast work at all during lightning risk, and anyone
already on a mast when weather turns comes down before finishing whatever they were
doing.

## The check-in call

Whoever is going out calls or messages another volunteer before setting off, saying
which stations are on the round and roughly when they expect to be back. A second
call goes out on the way home. If the return call hasn't come by an hour past the
stated time, the person who took the first call starts trying to reach them, and
after another half hour that becomes a call to whoever else is nearby enough to go
and look.

## What goes in the bag

Every round out to the stations carries a torch, a basic first-aid kit, a charged
phone, and enough warm layers for longer than the job should take, because jobs on
this network always take longer than planned. Spare desiccant sachets and a cloth go
in as standard now as well, given how often a box needs drying out on the spot.

## Livestock and gates

Several sites sit behind fields with livestock, and the rule there is simple: gates
get left exactly as found, shut if shut and open if open, and nobody crosses a field
with cattle in it if there's a way round. A locked gate means the job doesn't happen
that day rather than someone climbing over it.

## Electrics in the rain

Nobody opens a battery compartment or works on wiring while it's actively raining. If
a job can't wait for a dry spell, it gets done from under a tarp or not at all; there
is no job on this network that's worth doing wet-handed on a lead-acid terminal.
